'''William Andrew Goddard III''' (born March 29, 1937) is the Charles and Mary Ferkel Professor of Chemistry and Applied Physics, and director of the Materials and Process Simulation Center at the [[California Institute of Technology]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url = http://www.iaqms.org/members/goddard.php|title = William A. Goddard III|date = |access-date = 17 July 2014|website = |publisher = International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science|last = |first = }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=William A Goddard|url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=yMZlErUAAAAJ|website=Google Scholar |date = 2017}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
William A. Goddard III was born in El Centro California and lived his early years in farm towns across California (El Centro, Delano, Indio, Lodi, Oildale, MacFarland, Firebaugh, also Yuma AZ), where his dad made the wooden boxes used to ship agricultural products. He always dreamed of living in Los Angeles.<ref name="festschrift" /> Goddard earned a BS in engineering from the [[University of California at Los Angeles]] in 1960 and PhD in engineering science with a minor in physics from Caltech in 1964.<ref>{{Cite web|url = http://www.wag.caltech.edu/home/wag/|title = Prof. William A. Goddard III|date = |access-date = 17 July 2014|website = |publisher = Caltech Materials and Process Simulation Center|last = |first = }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=William A. Goddard|url=http://www.cce.caltech.edu/content/william-goddard|publisher=Caltech|date=2017|access-date=June 21, 2017|archive-date=June 23, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170623173554/http://cce.caltech.edu/content/william-goddard}}</ref>

He has four children (Bill, Suzy, Cecilia, Lisa) and has been married for 58 years. {{citation needed|date=October 2016}}

==Career==
He joined the chemistry faculty at Caltech in November 1964 where he remains today as a professor and researcher.

After his Ph.D. he remained at the [[California Institute of Technology]] as Arthur Amos Noyes Research Fellow (1964–66), Professor of Theoretical Chemistry (1967–78) and Professor of Chemistry & Applied Physics (1978-).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{cite web|title=William A. Goddard III|url=https://www.schrodinger.com/person/william-goddard-iii-phd|website=Schrodinger.com|date = 2017}}</ref>
Goddard has made many contributions to theoretical chemistry, such as the [[generalized valence bond]] (GVB) method for ''ab initio'' electronic structure calculations and the [[ReaxFF]] force field for classical molecular dynamics simulations. Goddard's consulting for industrial laboratories on practical problems — engine wear inhibitors, and corrosion, scale, and wax inhibitors in oil pipelines — led him to co-found several companies applying his group's simulation methods commercially.<ref name="scalacs">{{cite web|title=2000 Richard Chase Tolman Award: Dr. William A. Goddard, III, Caltech|url=https://scalacs.org/?page_id=1091|publisher=Southern California Section, American Chemical Society}}</ref> In 1984 he co-founded [[Molecular Simulations Inc.]] (later [[Accelrys]], now part of [[BIOVIA]]) together with his graduate student [[Stephen L. Mayo]], chairing its board from 1984 to 1991 and remaining a director until 1995.<ref name="cv">{{cite web|title=Curriculum Vitae: William A. Goddard III|url=http://wag.caltech.edu/home/wag/cv.html|publisher=California Institute of Technology}}</ref><ref name="mayo">{{cite web|title=Allogene Therapeutics Appoints Stephen Mayo to its Board of Directors|url=https://www.biospace.com/allogene-therapeutics-appoints-scientific-pioneer-stephen-mayo-to-its-board-of-directors|publisher=BioSpace|date=July 12, 2022}}</ref> In 1990 he co-founded [[Schrödinger, Inc.|Schrödinger]] with Columbia chemist [[Richard Friesner]], serving on its board of directors until 2000.<ref name="cv" /><ref name="cen">{{cite news|last=Jarvis|first=Lisa|title=Taking A Big Step In Virtual Space|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/89/i32/Taking-Big-Step-Virtual-Space.html|work=Chemical & Engineering News|date=2011}}</ref> He also co-founded Materials Research Source LLC, reorganized as Systine Inc. in 2003, and the bioinformatics company BionomiX Inc.<ref name="scalacs" /><ref name="cv" />

Goddard's later ventures moved toward biotechnology. In November 2005 he co-founded the Seattle-based company [[Allozyne]] with Caltech colleague [[David A. Tirrell]] and [[postdoctoral researcher]] Deepshikha Datta, commercializing a Caltech method for substituting non-natural amino acids into protein therapeutics to allow site-specific [[PEGylation]]; the company was launched out of the Accelerator Corporation incubator and raised a $30 million Series B in 2008.<ref name="bioworld">{{cite news|title=Biotech Allozyne Improving Protein Drugs With $30M Round|url=https://www.bioworld.com/articles/450115|work=BioWorld}}</ref><ref name="xconomy2008">{{cite news|last=Timmerman|first=Luke|title=Allozyne, Developer of Multiple Sclerosis Drug in Fewer Shots, Poised to Enter Clinical Trials|url=https://xconomy.com/seattle/2008/10/16/allozyne-developer-of-multiple-sclerosis-drug-in-fewer-shots-poised-to-enter-clinical-trials/|work=Xconomy|date=October 16, 2008}}</ref> In 2008 Accelerator backed a second company out of his laboratory, GPC-Rx, based on computational selection of drug candidates with improved target specificity.<ref>{{cite news|last=Timmerman|first=Luke|title=Accelerator Backs New Biotech Startup in Goddard Lab at Caltech|url=https://xconomy.com/seattle/2008/06/16/accelerator-backs-new-biotech-startup-in-goddard-lab-at-caltech/|work=Xconomy|date=June 16, 2008}}</ref>

He is a member of the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]] and the U.S. [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref name=":0" />

In August 2007, the [[American Chemical Society]] at its biannual national convention celebrated Goddard's 70th birthday with a 5-day symposium titled, "Bold predictions in theoretical chemistry."

As of November 2017, Goddard has published 1160 peer-reviewed articles.<ref>{{cite web |title=List of William A. Goddard published papers|url=http://www.wag.caltech.edu/publications/papers/|publisher=Caltech|date = 2017}}</ref>

==Research==
===Electronic structure theory===
Working with materials scientist [[Pol Duwez]] during his doctoral studies, Goddard developed a many-electron method built on eigenfunctions of total spin, published in a 1967 series in ''[[Physical Review]]'' as an improved quantum theory of many-electron systems.<ref name="ucla">{{cite web|title=William Goddard Honored with 2020 UCLA Samueli Lifetime Contribution Award|url=https://samueli.ucla.edu/william-goddard-honored-with-2020-ucla-samueli-lifetime-contribution-award/|publisher=UCLA Samueli School of Engineering|date=February 20, 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Goddard|first=William A. III|title=Improved Quantum Theory of Many-Electron Systems. II. The Basic Method|journal=Physical Review|year=1967|volume=157|issue=1|pages=81–93|doi=10.1103/PhysRev.157.81}}</ref> The approach became known as the [[generalized valence bond]] method, which UCLA has described as the first quantum mechanical method able to describe bond breaking and chemical reactions properly.<ref name="ucla" /> Because the full GVB equations were too costly for all but small systems, Goddard, [[William J. Hunt]] and [[P. Jeffrey Hay]] introduced in the early 1970s the GVB(PP/SO) approximation, which combines a perfect-pairing spin function with orthogonality between orbitals in different pairs; this form and the associated configuration interaction methods were applied widely through the early 1990s.<ref name="dunninghay">{{cite book|last1=Dunning|first1=Thom H. Jr.|last2=Hay|first2=P. Jeffrey|chapter=Beyond Molecular Orbital Theory: The Impact of Generalized Valence Bond Theory in Molecular Science|title=Computational Materials, Chemistry, and Biochemistry: From Bold Initiatives to the Last Mile|series=Springer Series in Materials Science|volume=284|publisher=Springer|location=Cham|year=2021|pages=55–87|doi=10.1007/978-3-030-18778-1_5|isbn=978-3-030-18777-4}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Goddard|first1=William A. III|last2=Dunning|first2=Thom H. Jr.|last3=Hunt|first3=William J.|last4=Hay|first4=P. Jeffrey|title=Generalized valence bond description of bonding in low-lying states of molecules|journal=Accounts of Chemical Research|year=1973|volume=6|issue=11|pages=368–376|doi=10.1021/ar50071a002}}</ref> Beginning in the 1970s his interests broadened from bonding in small molecules to semiconductor surfaces and heterogeneous catalysis.<ref name="ucla" />

===Force fields and reactive dynamics===
A second strand of Goddard's work has been the development of empirical and semi-empirical potentials intended to extend atomistic simulation to system sizes and timescales beyond the reach of quantum mechanics. With his students he introduced the DREIDING generic force field in 1990 and the Universal Force Field (UFF), parameterized across the full periodic table, in 1992, together with the charge equilibration (QEq) scheme for assigning atomic charges during a simulation.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mayo|first1=Stephen L.|last2=Olafson|first2=Barry D.|last3=Goddard|first3=William A. III|title=DREIDING: A generic force field for molecular simulations|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|year=1990|volume=94|issue=26|pages=8897–8909|doi=10.1021/j100389a010}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rappé|first1=A. K.|last2=Casewit|first2=C. J.|last3=Colwell|first3=K. S.|last4=Goddard|first4=W. A. III|last5=Skiff|first5=W. M.|title=UFF, a full periodic table force field for molecular mechanics and molecular dynamics simulations|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1992|volume=114|issue=25|pages=10024–10035|doi=10.1021/ja00051a040}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rappé|first1=Anthony K.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=Charge equilibration for molecular dynamics simulations|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry|year=1991|volume=95|issue=8|pages=3358–3363|doi=10.1021/j100161a070}}</ref> In 2001 Goddard and [[Adri van Duin]] introduced [[ReaxFF]], a bond-order force field fitted to quantum mechanical data that allows bonds to form and break during a classical molecular dynamics simulation, making reactive chemistry accessible at scales where explicit quantum treatments are impractical.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=van Duin|first1=Adri C. T.|last2=Dasgupta|first2=Siddharth|last3=Lorant|first3=Francois|last4=Goddard|first4=William A. III|title=ReaxFF: A Reactive Force Field for Hydrocarbons|journal=The Journal of Physical Chemistry A|year=2001|volume=105|issue=41|pages=9396–9409|doi=10.1021/jp004368u}}</ref>

===Matter under extreme conditions===
With his student Julius Su, Goddard introduced the electron force field (eFF) in 2007, an approximate solution of the time-dependent [[Schrödinger equation]] in which each electron is represented by a spherical Gaussian wave packet whose position and radius evolve dynamically. The method was designed to make nonadiabatic simulation of highly excited electronic systems tractable, and reproduced equations of state and single-shock [[Hugoniot]] curves for warm dense hydrogen up to 100,000 K.<ref name="eff">{{cite journal|last1=Su|first1=Julius T.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=Excited Electron Dynamics Modeling of Warm Dense Matter|journal=Physical Review Letters|year=2007|volume=99|issue=18|article-number=185003|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.185003}}</ref> Goddard and Su described applications ranging from [[Auger effect|Auger]] fragmentation in diamond nanoparticles to processes relevant to [[inertial confinement fusion]] and semiconductor device fabrication, and the method was subsequently used to study the high-temperature, high-pressure phases of lithium.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Su|first1=Julius T.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=The dynamics of highly excited electronic systems: Applications of the electron force field|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|year=2009|volume=131|issue=24|page=244501|doi=10.1063/1.3272671}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kim|first1=Hyungjun|last2=Su|first2=Julius T.|last3=Goddard|first3=William A. III|title=High-temperature high-pressure phases of lithium from electron force field (eFF) quantum electron dynamics simulations|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|year=2011|volume=108|issue=37|pages=15101–15105|doi=10.1073/pnas.1110322108|pmc=3174647}}</ref> eFF belongs to the wave packet molecular dynamics family and has been taken up by other groups working on [[warm dense matter]] and dense plasmas.

===Atomic theory and effective core potentials===
Goddard's 1967–69 series in ''[[Physical Review]]'' applied his spin-eigenfunction formalism, then called the GI or G1 method, to atoms as well as molecules, producing correlated atomic wavefunctions that retained an orbital interpretation.<ref name="dunninghay" /> Building on those atomic calculations, Goddard and his student Carl Melius introduced a practical scheme for replacing an atom's chemically inert core electrons with an analytic effective potential fitted to ''ab initio'' atomic wavefunctions, first in 1972 with Lawrence Kahn and then in a 1974 formulation designed to exploit the properties of Gaussian basis functions.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Melius|first1=C. F.|last2=Kahn|first2=L. R.|last3=Goddard|first3=W. A. III|title=Ab Initio Effective Potentials for Use in Molecular Calculations|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|year=1972|volume=56|issue=6|pages=2685–2689|doi=10.1063/1.1677596}}</ref><ref name="ecp">{{cite journal|last1=Melius|first1=C. F.|last2=Goddard|first2=W. A. III|title=Ab initio effective potentials for use in molecular quantum mechanics|journal=Physical Review A|year=1974|volume=10|issue=5|pages=1528–1540|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.10.1528}}</ref> Because the cost of an all-electron calculation grows steeply with atomic number, the method made heavy elements tractable, and it was extended to the transition metals iron and nickel the same year.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Melius|first1=C. F.|last2=Olafson|first2=B. D.|last3=Goddard|first3=W. A. III|title=Fe and Ni ab initio effective potentials for use in molecular calculations|journal=Chemical Physics Letters|year=1974|volume=28|issue=4|pages=457–462|doi=10.1016/0009-2614(74)80079-5}}</ref> Subsequent relativistic effective core potentials, including those of Lee, Ermler and [[Kenneth Pitzer|Pitzer]], were built on the Goddard–Melius treatment together with that of Kahn, Baybutt and [[Donald Truhlar|Truhlar]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Lee|first1=Yoon S.|last2=Ermler|first2=Walter C.|last3=Pitzer|first3=Kenneth S.|title=Ab initio effective core potentials including relativistic effects. I. Formalism and applications to the Xe and Au atoms|journal=The Journal of Chemical Physics|year=1977|volume=67|issue=12|pages=5861–5876|doi=10.1063/1.434793}}</ref>

===Biomolecular structure prediction===
From the late 1990s Goddard's group extended its simulation methods to biological systems, concentrating on [[G protein-coupled receptor]]s (GPCRs), the receptor superfamily that mediates vision, smell, taste and pain and that accounts for a large share of drug targets. At the time an experimental atomic-level structure existed for only one GPCR, bovine [[rhodopsin]], which blocked structure-based drug design for the rest of the family. Goddard and his co-workers developed MembStruk, a first-principles procedure for predicting the three-dimensional structure of a helical membrane protein from sequence, and HierDock, a hierarchical method for predicting where a ligand binds and how strongly.<ref name="gpcr2002">{{cite journal|last1=Vaidehi|first1=Nagarajan|last2=Floriano|first2=Wely B.|last3=Trabanino|first3=Rene|last4=Hall|first4=Spencer E.|last5=Freddolino|first5=Peter|last6=Choi|first6=Eun Jung|last7=Zamanakos|first7=Georgios|last8=Goddard|first8=William A. III|title=Prediction of structure and function of G protein-coupled receptors|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|year=2002|volume=99|issue=20|pages=12622–12627|doi=10.1073/pnas.122357199|pmid=12351677|pmc=130510}}</ref> Validating the methods against rhodopsin, they reported predicted structures and binding sites for the β1-adrenergic receptor, endothelial differentiation gene 6, the mouse and rat I7 olfactory receptors and the human sweet receptor, with the predicted epinephrine site in β1-adrenergic receptor matching mutation experiments.<ref name="gpcr2002" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Trabanino|first1=Rene J.|last2=Hall|first2=Spencer E.|last3=Vaidehi|first3=Nagarajan|last4=Floriano|first4=Wely B.|last5=Kam|first5=Victor W. T.|last6=Goddard|first6=William A. III|title=First principles predictions of the structure and function of G-protein-coupled receptors: validation for bovine rhodopsin|journal=Biophysical Journal|year=2004|volume=86|issue=4|pages=1904–1921|doi=10.1016/S0006-3495(04)74256-3|pmid=15041637|pmc=1304048}}</ref> The protein calculations used the group's own DREIDING force field and QEq charges, an example of the methodological chain running from Goddard's force-field work into biology.<ref name="gpcr2002" />

===Catalysis and surfaces===
With Anthony Rappé, Goddard proposed in the early 1980s that high-valent Group VI [[olefin metathesis]] catalysts operate through metal–oxo rather than purely alkylidene intermediates, and analyzed the mechanistic relationship between metathesis and epoxidation in chromium and molybdenum complexes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rappé|first1=Anthony K.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=Mechanism of metathesis and epoxidation in chromium and molybdenum complexes containing methyl-oxo bonds|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1980|volume=102|issue=15|pages=5114–5115|doi=10.1021/ja00535a058}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rappé|first1=Anthony K.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=Olefin metathesis—a mechanistic study of high-valent Group VI catalysts|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1982|volume=104|issue=2|pages=448–456|doi=10.1021/ja00366a013}}</ref> He had earlier formulated the orbital phase continuity principle, a set of selection rules for concerted reactions derived from valence bond rather than molecular orbital reasoning.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Goddard|first=William A. III|title=Selection rules for chemical reactions using the orbital phase continuity principle|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1972|volume=94|issue=3|pages=793–807|doi=10.1021/ja00758a019}}</ref> His group also used nickel clusters of increasing size to model chemisorption on metal surfaces, work that fed the shift of his research toward semiconductor surfaces and heterogeneous catalysis.<ref name="ucla" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Upton|first1=Thomas H.|last2=Goddard|first2=William A. III|title=Chemisorption of atomic hydrogen on large scale nickel cluster surfaces|journal=Physical Review Letters|year=1979|volume=42|issue=7|pages=472–476|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.42.472}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
Goddard was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]] in 1984 and to the [[International Academy of Quantum Molecular Science]] in 1988. He is a fellow of the [[American Physical Society]] (1988), the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] (1990), the [[Royal Society of Chemistry]] (2008) and the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] (2010). His awards include the [[American Chemical Society]] Award for Computers in Chemistry (1988), Caltech's Richard M. Badger Teaching Prize in Chemistry (1995), the [[Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology|Foresight Institute Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology]] for theory (1999, shared with Tahir Cagin and [[Yue Qi]] for modeling molecular machines), a NASA Space Sciences Award (2000), the Richard Chase Tolman Medal of the Southern California Section of the ACS (2000), an honorary doctorate from [[Uppsala University]] (2004) and the ACS Award in Theoretical Chemistry (2007).<ref name=":0" /><ref name="scalacs" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology 1999|url=https://www.foresight.org/2018/12/03/1999-feynman-prize-in-nanotechnology/|publisher=Foresight Institute}}</ref>
